(p-212) Sūrat Luqmān is Makkī except for one verse, which is "Those who establish the prayer and give the zakāt" (﴿Alladhīna yuqīmūnaṣ-ṣalāta wa yu'tūnaz-zakāt﴾). Their obligation was [revealed] at Madīnah, but this view is weak, because it does not preclude that they were legislated in Makkah. It is also said that the exception is three phrases from His saying ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens﴾, which amounts to thirty-four verses. It is also said thirty-three.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾ Its explanation has preceded in Sūrat Yūnus.

﴿A guidance and a mercy for the good-doers.﴾ These are two circumstantial clauses (ḥāl) from "the verses," and the operative element in them is the meaning of indication (ishārah). Ḥamzah read them in the nominative, either as a second predicate after the first predicate, or as predicates of an omitted subject.

**Qur'an 31:4–5:** ﴿Those who establish the prayer, and give the zakat, and are certain of the Hereafter.﴾ This is an explanation of their excellence (iḥsān), or a specification of these three from among its branches, due to the special esteem given to them. The repetition of the pronoun (hum) is for emphasis, and because a separation has been placed between it and its predicate.

﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.﴾ (This is) because they combine the true creed and righteous action.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 6:

﴿And among people is one who buys idle talk﴾ : that which distracts from what matters, such as tales that have no basis, legends that carry no lesson, jokes, and superfluous speech. The construction (idafah, genitive construction) is in the sense of "min" (from/of). It is explicative (bayaniyyah) if by "talk" is meant the reprehensible kind, and partitive (tab'idiyyah) if by it is meant the more general category that includes it. It was said that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who bought the books of the non-Arabs and would relate them to the Quraysh, saying: "If Muhammad tells you of the story of 'Ad and Thamud, then I will tell you of the story of Rustam, Isfandiyar and the Kisras (Sasanian kings)." It was also said that he would buy singing slave-girls and have them entertain those who wished to embrace Islam, to keep them away from it. ﴿so that he may lead astray from the way of God﴾ : from His religion or from the recitation of His Book. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha on the ya' (yudilla, meaning "that he may remain in his error and increase in it"). ﴿without knowledge﴾ : regarding the state of what he buys, or in the sense of "without a trade," since he exchanged the recitation of the Qur'an for idle talk. ﴿and takes it in mockery﴾ : and takes the way (of God) as a mockery. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Hafs put it in the accusative, coordinating it with (li-yudilla, "so that he may lead astray"). ﴿For them there is a humiliating punishment﴾ : because of their humiliating the truth by giving preference to falsehood over it.(p-213)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 7:

﴿And when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away arrogantly﴾ mutakabbiran (proud, haughty), not regarding them. ﴿As if he had not heard them﴾ resembling in his state the state of one who has not heard them. ﴿As if there were in his ears a deafness﴾ resembling one who has a heaviness in his ears, unable to hear. The first (clause) is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun concealed in ﴿wallā﴾ or in ﴿mustakbiran﴾, and the second is a substitute (badal) for it, or a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun concealed in ﴿lam yasma'hā﴾; it is also permissible that both be resumptive clauses (isti'nafayn). Nafi' recited ﴿fī udhunayhi﴾. ﴿So give him tidings of a painful punishment﴾: inform him that punishment will surely befall him, and he mentioned "tidings" sarcastically (tahakkum).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verses 8–9:

﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds will have gardens of bliss.﴾ That is, they will have the bliss of the gardens; the construction is reversed (ʿaks) for the sake of emphasis (mubalagha).

﴿Abiding therein eternally﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in ﴿for them﴾, or to ﴿gardens of bliss﴾; and the governing element (ʿāmil) is what the preposition (lām) is attached to. ﴿A promise of Allah, true﴾: both are verbal nouns (maṣdar) functioning as emphatic (muʾakkid) elements; the first emphasizes itself, and the second emphasizes something else, because the statement ﴿for them are gardens﴾ is a promise, and not every promise is true.

﴿And He is the Mighty (al-ʿAzīz)﴾, the One whom nothing overcomes so as to prevent Him from fulfilling His promise and His threat. ﴿The Wise (al-Ḥakīm)﴾, the One who does only what His wisdom requires.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verses 10–11:

﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾. It has already been discussed in "al-Ra'd" (Surah 13). ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾, i.e., lofty mountains.

﴿Lest it should shake with you﴾: that is, lest it should shake with you. The sameness of its parts requires that their locations and positions be interchangeable, since it is impossible for any one of them to be specifically assigned, by its own essence or by any of its necessary attributes, to a particular place and a particular position. ﴿And He scattered throughout it creatures of every kind, and We sent down water from the sky and caused every noble pair of plants to grow therein﴾: every kind that is abundant in benefit. It seems that He used this as evidence of His might, which is the perfection of power, and His wisdom, which is the perfection of knowledge, and by it He laid the groundwork for the principle of monotheism and established it with His words:

﴿This is the creation of God; so show me what those other than Him have created﴾. This refers to what He has mentioned as His creation: so what have your gods created, that they should deserve to share in His dominion? The word "ma" (what) is either in the accusative governed by "khalq" (creation), or it is a nominative subject ("ma" as mubtada') whose predicate is "dha" (this) together with its relative clause, and "fa-arunī" (then show me) is suspended from it. ﴿Rather, the wrongdoers are in manifest error﴾: this is a turning away from rebuking them to recording against them an error that is not hidden from any observer. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that they are wrongdoers by their associating partners with God.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 12:

﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾. He is Luqman son of Ba'ura, of the descendants of Azar, the son of the sister of Ayyub (Job) or his maternal aunt's son. He lived until he reached Dawud (David), upon him be peace, and took knowledge from him, and he used to give legal rulings (yufti) before his mission (mab'ath). The majority are of the view that he was a wise man (hakim) and was not a prophet (nabi).

The wisdom (al-hikmah) in the terminology of the scholars (ulama') is: the perfecting of the human soul through acquiring theoretical sciences, and acquiring a complete disposition (malakah) over virtuous actions to the extent of one's capacity. Among his wisdom is that he accompanied Dawud for months, and he would weave the coat of mail (yasrudu al-dir'), and [Dawud] did not ask him about it. When he had finished it, he put it on and said: "How excellent a garment of war you are." [Luqman] said: "Silence is a wisdom, and few are those who practise it." Also, Dawud, upon him be peace, said to him one day: "How did you wake up?" He said: "I woke up in the hand of another." Dawud reflected upon this and swooned in a faint. He also commanded him to slaughter a sheep and bring the two best morsels from it, so he brought the tongue and the heart. Then, after some days, he commanded him to bring the two worst morsels from it, so he brought these two as well. [Dawud] asked him about that, and he said: "They are the best of things when they are good, and the worst of things when they are corrupt."

﴿That give thanks to God﴾, because "an" (that) is interpreted as "ashkur" (I give thanks) or "ay" (namely) "ashkuru", since the giving of wisdom is in the sense of speech. ﴿And whoever gives thanks, he gives thanks only for his own soul﴾, because its benefit returns to it, namely the continuance of the blessing and the deserving of its increase. ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed God is Self-Sufficient﴾, not needing thanks, ﴿Praiseworthy﴾, deserving of praise even if He is not praised, or [it means] One who is praised, all His creatures declaring His praise by the tongue of their state.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 13:

﴿And when Luqman said to his son﴾ — An'am, or Ashkam, or Mathan. ﴿while he was admonishing him: "O my little son"﴾ — a diminutive expressing affection and compassion. Ibn Kathir recited here and in ﴿"O my little son, establish the prayer"﴾ with the ya' sukun (silent), and Hafs recited both of these and in ﴿"O my little son, indeed it [the deed] be [as small as] the weight of a mustard seed"﴾ with the ya' fathah (open), and al-Bazzi did likewise in the last one, while the rest recited all three with the ya' kasrah (kasr). ﴿"Do not associate anything with Allah"﴾ — it was said that he was a disbeliever, and he kept at him until he became a Muslim. Whoever pauses at ( do not associate ) makes "with Allah" an oath. ﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a great injustice﴾ — because it equates between one from whom there is no blessing except from Him and one from whom there is no blessing at all.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 14:

﴿And We have enjoined upon man (concerning) his parents. His mother bore him in weakness upon weakness﴾ (wahnan), meaning: she bore him in a state of weakness, or she herself grows weak, weakness (wahnan). ﴿upon weakness﴾, that is, she grows weaker, weakness upon weakness, for her weakness continues to multiply. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal). It has also been read with vowelling of the middle letter (wahan): one says wahana yahinu wahnan and wahana yuhinu wahnan.

﴿And his weaning is in two years﴾ (fisaluhu), that is, his weaning (fitamuhu) at the end of two years, and she would nurse him during that period. It has also been read "wa fasluhu fi 'amayn" (wa fasluhu). In this there is evidence that the maximum period of breastfeeding is two years.

﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾ (an ushkur li wa li-walidayk). This is an explanation of (wassayna) or a reason for it, or a substitute for "his parents" as a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). The mention of the carrying and weaning in between is a parenthetical insertion emphasizing the enjoinment concerning her in particular; and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the one who asked, "Who is most deserving of my good companionship?": "Your mother, then your mother, then your mother, then (your father)."

﴿To Me is the final return﴾, so I will hold you accountable for your gratitude and your ingratitude.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 15:

﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge﴾ — that they have the right to be associated [with Him], out of mere imitation of them both. It is also said that by the negation of knowledge of it, what is meant is the negation of its existence. ﴿Then do not obey them﴾ in that. ﴿And keep company with them in this world kindly﴾ — companionship that is kind, which the Sharia approves and generosity requires. ﴿And follow﴾ in religion ﴿the way of him who turns to Me﴾ in repentance, by affirming the Oneness of God and sincerity in obedience. ﴿Then to Me is your return﴾ — your return and their return. ﴿Then I will inform you of what you used to do﴾ — by rewarding you for your faith and rewarding them for their disbelief. The two verses are parenthetical within the counsel of Luqman, emphasizing what it contains of the prohibition of associating partners, as if he said: "We have enjoined the like of what he enjoined." He mentioned the parents to intensify this, for although they come after the Creator in deserving reverence and obedience, they may not be obeyed in associating partners; so what do you think of others besides them? These verses were revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his mother, who remained for three days without eating anything when he embraced Islam. For this reason, it is said that "him who turns to Me" refers to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), for he embraced Islam through his call.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 16:

﴿O my son, indeed it, if it should be the weight of a mustard seed﴾ meaning: the matter of good or evil, if it should be, by way of example, as small as a mustard seed. Nafi' read ﴿mithqala﴾ in the nominative, with the pronoun (ha') referring to the matter (al-qissa, "the narrative/affair"), and the verb (kana) is then complete (taammah, i.e., it needs no predicate), and its feminine marking is because the mithqal is attached to the grain (habba), as in the words of the poet:

"As the spear's head was reddened by the blood" (p-215)

Or because what is intended by it is the good deed or the evil deed. ﴿Then it would be in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth﴾ in the most hidden and most secure place, such as the inside of a rock, or its top, like the arching of the heavens, or its bottom, like the hollow of the earth. It was also read with the kasra on the kaf, from (wakana), when a bird settles in its nest (wukna). ﴿Allah will bring it forth﴾ He will produce it, and so He will call it to account for it. ﴿Indeed Allah is Subtle﴾ His knowledge reaches every hidden thing. ﴿Aware﴾ knowing its reality.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 17:

﴿O my son, establish the prayer﴾ for the perfection of yourself. ﴿And enjoin what is right﴾ and forbid what is wrong, for the perfection of others. ﴿And endure what befalls you﴾ of hardships, especially in that. ﴿Indeed, that﴾ is a reference to patience, or to everything He has commanded. ﴿Is of the matters requiring resolve﴾ of what Allah has made binding (ʿazm) of matters, i.e., He has decreed it with a decisive decree. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used in the sense of the passive participle (maʿzūm, "resolved upon"). It is also permissible that it be in the sense of the active participle, from His saying ﴿and when the matter is resolved upon﴾, i.e., becomes serious (jadd).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verses 18–19:

﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people﴾ (lā tuṣaʿʿir khaddaka lil-nās): do not incline it away from them, nor turn the side of your face toward them as the arrogant do, out of ṣaʿar (a disease that afflicts the camel so that it twists its neck). Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read "wa lā tuṣā'ir" (with an alif), and it was also read "wa lā taṣʿar." All of these are one in meaning, like ʿulāhu, aʿlāhu and ʿālāhu. ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾: maraḥan is a verbal noun (maṣdar) occupying the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning "exulting," i.e., you walk exulting, or for the sake of exultation, which is insolence (baṭar). ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾: this is the reason for the prohibition. The mention of "boastful" (fakhūr) after "arrogant" (mukhtāl) is placed in contrast to the one who turns his cheek away, and mukhtāl is for one who walks exultantly, for the sake of harmony among the verse-endings (ru'ūs al-āy).

﴿And be moderate in your walk﴾: be intermediate in it, between the slow pace (dabīb) and hastening.

And from him, peace and blessings be upon him: "The haste of walking removes the radiance of the believer." And ʿĀʾishah's saying about ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both: "When he walked, he hastened." So what is meant is more than the slow pace of one feigning frailty. It was also read with a hamzah cut from aqṣada (the archer), when he aims his arrow straight toward the target.

﴿And lower your voice﴾: and diminish it, reduce it, and shorten it. ﴿Indeed, the most hideous of voices﴾: the most frightening of them. ﴿is the braying of donkeys﴾: the donkey is a proverbial example in censure, especially its bray, and for this reason it is referred to indirectly, as when one says "long-eared." The representation of a raised voice by its own sound, and then presenting it as a metaphor, is an intense exaggeration. The word "voice" is singular because the intent is to declare the category (jins) as the most objectionable, not the individual instances; or because it is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 20:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens﴾ by making them means that produce your benefits. ﴿and whatever is in the earth﴾ by enabling you to benefit from it, either through an intermediary or without one. ﴿And He has lavished upon you His favours, outward and inward﴾, sensible and intelligible, those you know and those you do not know. The explanation and detailing of the favour has already been discussed in al-Fatihah. It has also been read as "wa-asbagha" (with substitution), which applies to every sin that comes together with a ghayn, khaʼ or qaf, as in ṣalakha and ṣaqara. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Hafs read "niʻmatahu" (in the singular, with a pronoun suffix) as "niʻamahu" (in the plural, with a pronoun suffix).

﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah﴾ concerning His oneness and His attributes. ﴿without knowledge﴾ derived from proof. ﴿nor guidance﴾ traced back to a messenger. ﴿nor an enlightening Book﴾ sent down by Allah, but rather by imitation (taqlid), as He says:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verses 21–22:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon."﴾ This is a clear prohibition of taqlid (blind imitation, i.e., following others without evidence) in matters of the fundamentals (usul). ﴿What! Even if Satan was inviting them﴾ The pronoun may refer to them and to their fathers. ﴿To the punishment of the blazing Fire﴾ That is, to what their taqlid or polytheism leads to. The answer to "law" (law, "even if") is omitted, the equivalent of "they would have followed him." The interrogation is for denunciation and wonder.

﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ That is, he entrusts his affair to Him and turns wholeheartedly toward Him, taken from "aslamtu al-mata' ila al-zabun" (I handed over the goods to the buyer). The reading with the doubled letter (shadda) supports this. Its construction with the preposition "li" (for/to) is because it implies the meaning of sincerity (ikhlas). ﴿While he is a doer of good﴾ in his deeds. ﴿Then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾ He has clung to the strongest thing one can cling to. This is an illustration of the one who trusts in God and is occupied with obedience, likened to a man who wishes to climb to the summit of a high mountain and grips the strongest loops of the rope hanging down from it. ﴿And to Allah is the outcome of affairs﴾ since everything returns to Him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verses 21–22:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon."﴾ This is a clear prohibition of taqlid (blind imitation, i.e., following others without evidence) in matters of the fundamentals (usul). ﴿What! Even if Satan was inviting them﴾ The pronoun may refer to them and to their fathers. ﴿To the punishment of the blazing Fire﴾ That is, to what their taqlid or polytheism leads to. The answer to "law" (law, "even if") is omitted, the equivalent of "they would have followed him." The interrogation is for denunciation and wonder.

﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ That is, he entrusts his affair to Him and turns wholeheartedly toward Him, taken from "aslamtu al-mata' ila al-zabun" (I handed over the goods to the buyer). The reading with the doubled letter (shadda) supports this. Its construction with the preposition "li" (for/to) is because it implies the meaning of sincerity (ikhlas). ﴿While he is a doer of good﴾ in his deeds. ﴿Then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾ He has clung to the strongest thing one can cling to. This is an illustration of the one who trusts in God and is occupied with obedience, likened to a man who wishes to climb to the summit of a high mountain and grips the strongest loops of the rope hanging down from it. ﴿And to Allah is the outcome of affairs﴾ since everything returns to Him.

﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you.﴾ For it does not harm you in this world or in the Hereafter. It was also read as «فَلا يَحْزَنْكَ» (falā yaḥzanka), from the causative aḥzana, but this reading (qirā'a) is not widely transmitted (mustafīḍ). ﴿To Us is their return﴾ in both abodes. ﴿Then We will inform them of what they did﴾ by destruction and punishment. ﴿Indeed Allah is Knower of what is in the breasts﴾, so He will recompense for it, let alone for what is apparent.

﴿We will let them enjoy briefly﴾, either as an enjoyment or for a brief period, since what passes away is little compared to what endures. ﴿Then We will compel them to a harsh punishment﴾ that weighs upon them like the weight of heavy bodies, or that adds compression (al-ḍaghṭ) to burning. Here «نَضْطَرُّهم» (naḍṭarruhum) means "We will force them" or "drive them," from the form iḍṭarra.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verses 25–26:

﴿And if you were to ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "God."﴾ (This is) because the proof that prevents attributing creation to anything else is so clear that they are compelled to acknowledge it. ﴿Say: "Praise be to God"﴾ for silencing them and forcing them to admit what necessitates the invalidity of their belief.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that this obliges them.

﴿To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾; none in them deserves worship other than Him. ﴿Indeed, God is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghaniyy)﴾ above the praise of those who praise (Him).

﴿the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid)﴾: the one who deserves praise even if He is not praised.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 27:

﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾ — even if it were established that the trees are pens, the singular "tree" (shajarah) is used because the intent is the detailing of individual units.

﴿And the sea, with seven more seas to replenish it﴾ — the surrounding sea, with its vastness, would be ink extended by seven seas; he dispensed with mentioning the ink by saying "yamudduhu" (replenishes it), since it derives from madda al-dawah wa amaddaha (he extended the inkwell and supplied it). He put it in the nominative (rafa'ahu) either by coordinating it with the position (mahall) of inna and its two operands, and "yamuddu-hu" is a circumstantial clause (hal), or it is a beginning (ibtida') as an independent resumption (mustaʼnaf), or the waw is for the circumstantial clause. The Basran grammarians put it in the accusative (nasabahu) by coordination with the noun of inna (ism inna), or by assuming a verb that is explained by "yamuddu-hu." It has also been read as "tamuddu-hu" and "wa-yamuddu-hu" with the ya' and the ta'.

﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ — by writing them with those pens and that ink. The choice of the plural of paucity (jam' qillah) for the (pens and seas) is to indicate that this would not suffice for the few, let alone the many.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty﴾ — nothing overcomes Him.

﴿Wise﴾ — no matter escapes His knowledge and wisdom.

The verse is a reply to the Jews, who asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or who instructed the delegation of Quraysh to ask him, about His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾. Yet He had sent down the Torah, and in it is the knowledge of everything.

Your creation and your resurrection are only like [that of] a single soul, ﴿ما خَلْقُكم ولا بَعْثُكم إلا كَنَفْسٍ واحِدَةٍ﴾, that is, like its creation and its resurrection. Nothing diverts Him from one affair to another. The existence of all things suffices by the connection of His necessary will (*irada wajiba*, the will that must be realized) together with His essential power (*qudra dhatiyya*), as He said: ﴿Indeed, Our command for a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is.﴾

﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing﴾, who hears everything that can be heard, ﴿All-Seeing﴾, who sees everything that can be seen. The perception of some things does not occupy Him from others, and likewise is His creation.

﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and has subjected the sun and the moon, each running [in its orbit] until a specified term﴾. Each of the two luminaries runs in its orbit. ﴿Until a specified term﴾ means until a known limit: for the sun, until the end of the year, and for the moon, until the end of the month.

It is also said: until the Day of Resurrection. The difference between this phrase and His words ﴿for a specified term﴾ is that the *ajal* (term, appointed end) here is the end of the motion, whereas there its purpose (*gharad*) is literal or figurative. Both meanings are found in ends. ﴿And that Allah is Aware of what you do﴾, knowing its reality.

﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned: the vastness of knowledge, the comprehensiveness of power, the wonders of creation, and the exclusivity of the Creator with them.

﴿Because Allah is the Truth﴾, by reason of His being the one established in His essence, necessary in every respect, or the one whose divinity is established. ﴿And that what they call upon besides Him﴾ is the falsehood, nonexistent in itself, because it is neither brought into being nor characterized except by His making it so; or the falsehood is its divinity. The Basrans and the Kufans, except Abu Bakr, read *yad'una* with the letter *ya'* (the third-person form), while the others read *tad'una* with *ta'* (the second-person form). ﴿And that Allah is the Most High, the Great﴾, exalted above everything and dominant over it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verses 31–32:

﴿Have you not seen that the ship sails on the sea by the favour of God﴾, by His beneficence in preparing its means. This is another proof of His manifest power, the perfection of His wisdom, and the comprehensiveness of His bounty. The bā' (in bi-ni'mati) is either for attachment (ṣila) or for circumstance (ḥāl). It has been read as "al-fulk" with a doubled lām, and as "bi-ni'māti Llāh" with a sukūn on the ʿayn. In its like, kasra, fatḥa and sukūn are all permitted. ﴿That He may show you of His signs﴾, meaning His proofs. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every ṣabbār﴾, one who is patient in hardships, so he exhausts himself in reflecting upon the horizons and upon the self. ﴿Shakūr﴾, one who recognises blessings and considers their Giver; or [it refers] to the believers, for faith is two halves: half patience and half gratitude.

﴿And when a wave covers them﴾, overtakes and envelops them. ﴿Like shades (ẓulal)﴾, as one is shaded by a mountain, a cloud, or other things. It has been read as "kal-ẓilāl", the plural of ẓulla, like qilla and qilāl. ﴿They call upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾, because of the removal of what contests the primordial nature (fiṭra) from caprice and imitation, through the great fear that has befallen them. ﴿But when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate﴾, remaining upon the middle path, which is monotheism; or one who is intermediate in disbelief, since he is restrained to some degree of restraint. ﴿And none deny Our signs except every treacherous ungrateful one﴾, a betrayer, for this is a breach of the primordial covenant; or, since what occurred at sea was [a matter of] treachery, the greatest treachery is that of [one who is] ungrateful. ﴿Ungrateful (kafūr)﴾, to the blessings.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 33:

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord and dread a Day when no father will avail anything for his child﴾ (i.e., will not settle anything on his behalf), and it is read "lā yujzi'u" (from ajza'a, meaning "to suffice, to be enough"). The pronoun referring back to the described noun is omitted, meaning: no one is recompensed for anything on it. ﴿Nor will a child avail anything for his father﴾ — it is either coordinated with "father" (wālidun), or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿is one who avails anything for his father﴾. The alteration of the structure serves to indicate that the child is more deserving of not availing (for his father), and to cut off the hope of those among the believers who expected that he might benefit his unbelieving father in the Hereafter. ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah﴾ — of reward and punishment — ﴿is true﴾, its breach being impossible.

﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you, and let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾ — the Satan — by making you hope for repentance and forgiveness, so that he emboldens you towards sins.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 34:

﴿Indeed, Allah has with Him the knowledge of the Hour﴾: the knowledge of its time of establishment. This is because it was narrated that "al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'When is the establishment of the Hour? I have cast my seeds into the earth, so when will the sky rain? And my wife's pregnancy, is it male or female? What will I do tomorrow, and where will I die?' So this was revealed."

And on his authority, peace be upon him: "The keys of the Unseen are five," and he recited this verse. ﴿And He sends down the rain﴾ at its appointed time that is determined for it and in the specific place designated for it in His knowledge. Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim read it with the shaddah (yunazzilu, intensive form). ﴿And He knows what is in the wombs﴾: whether it is male or female, complete or deficient. ﴿And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow﴾ of good or evil, and it may resolve upon something and then do the opposite of it. ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾, just as it does not know at what time it will die.

It was reported that the Angel of Death passed by Sulaymān (peace be upon him), and began to look at a man among his companions, gazing at him for a long time. The man said, "Who is this?" He said, "The Angel of Death." The man said, "It seems he wants me. So command the wind to carry me and cast me down in India." He did so. The angel then said, "My prolonged gaze at him was out of wonder, for I was commanded to seize his soul in India, and he was with you." 

He made knowledge ('ilm) belong to Allah, the Exalted, and made dirāyah (knowledge acquired through reasoning and investigation) belong to the servant, because it carries the sense of contrivance (ḥīlah), so one perceives the difference between the two kinds of knowledge. It also indicates that if a person devises a stratagem and exerts his utmost effort in it, he still does not know what is the truth in it from his own acquisition and its outcome; so how about other matters for which no evidence has been set up? It was also read as "bi-ayyati arḍin" (in which land). Sībawayh likened the feminine marking of it to the feminine marking of kull in (kulluhunna). ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing﴾, who knows all things. ﴿All-Aware﴾, who knows their inner aspects just as He knows their outer aspects.

On his authority, peace be upon him: "Whoever recites Surah Luqmān, Luqmān will be his companion on the Day of Resurrection, and he will be given ten good deeds for each person who acted upon what is right and forbade what is wrong."
